From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter

## Overall assessment

The Seller's package is not balanced. It is built to move almost all known risk onto the Buyer and to limit the Buyer's recourse for anything it does not know about. Several known issues (Riverlark, Bluefen, Ironquay, the employee bonuses, the privacy incident) are identified in the Disclosure Letter but left unresolved, and the proposed limits would make it hard to recover on them through warranty claims. Read together, the Seller's terms would mean the Buyer carries:

- the known exposures, through the funds flow, conditions, and "reasonable endeavours" language;
- the unknown exposures, through a low cap, a deductible basket, and short time limits; and
- the risk of anything in the data room, because of the general disclosure and knowledge bar.

Note: I have reviewed the Seller's summary and Disclosure Letter only. I have not reviewed the underlying DD-002 to DD-012 documents, the full SPA, or the funds flow. The NSW and Commonwealth law points below should be confirmed by the deal team's counsel before they are put to the Seller.

---

## 1. Risk allocation and recourse (Clauses 12.1, 12.2, 12.3/13, 12.8, 9.3, 20.5)

**General cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m).** A cap of one-fifth of the price is low for general warranties in a transaction of this size. It is also below the quantified known exposures (see section 3), so the Buyer could be exposed beyond the cap on known issues and recover little. Push for a general cap of at least 100% of the price, with a lower cap (commonly 10–20%) only as a trade for other concessions.

**Basket structured as an excess-only deductible (AUD 250k).** Under this structure, the Buyer bears the first AUD 250k of losses. The Buyer should seek a tipping basket, under which once the threshold is crossed the Buyer recovers from the first dollar. Also:
- The AUD 25k de minimis should be reduced (for example, to AUD 5k), and related claims should be aggregated so they cannot be split below the threshold.
- Claims arising from the same facts should count as one claim.

**Time limits (18 months general; extended to "all Claims").** Eighteen months does not cover a full audit or tax cycle, or the period in which privacy and contractual disputes usually emerge. The Seller's drafting would also apply the general period to fundamental, title, and tax claims. Push for:
- general warranties: 36 months;
- tax: until 60 days after the relevant ATO assessment period closes (subject to the statutory position);
- title and capacity: at least six years, which matches the general NSW contract limitation period (Limitation Act 1969 (NSW)), or longer if the SPA is executed as a deed.

**Fundamental and title warranties on general caps and time limits.** The Seller's "administrative simplicity" rationale does not justify this. Title, capacity, and authority warranties should be capped at the full purchase price and should survive for the longer period above. The Buyer is buying 100% of the shares, so title is fundamental to the transaction.

**Exclusive remedy, limitations, and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (9.3, 12.8, 20.5).** This language would sweep in fraud, specific indemnities, price adjustments, and funds flow shortfalls. Reject it. Carve out:
- fraud and dishonesty;
- fundamental and tax warranties;
- specific indemnities;
- price and completion adjustments.

Non-reliance language is generally acceptable in Australia, but it should not exclude claims based on fraud or on the warranties actually given.

---

## 2. Disclosure and knowledge (Schedule 7, Disclosure Letter 1.1 and 1.2, Clause 8.3)

**General disclosure of the entire data room (1.1) and public registers (1.2).** This is the most serious issue in the package. If the Seller's letter were accepted, every fact in the data room (currently DD-002 to DD-012, and presumably more) and every entry on public registers would qualify the warranties. That would hollow out the warranty package. Disclosure should be:
- specific, referring to particular warranties;
- fairly disclosed, meaning the Buyer can understand the matter and its significance from the disclosure itself; and
- limited to the documents the Buyer has actually been given, at the relevant date.

Reject general disclosure. Public searches should not be deemed disclosure against warranties about title, registration, or encumbrances. The Buyer should run its own searches and rely on the warranties.

**Disclosure date.** The letter speaks as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026. Today is 5 November 2026. Require a fresh disclosure letter and data room index, brought down to signing and Completion. Any new matter should be disclosed in writing, with the Buyer's right to walk or re-price if it is material.

**Buyer knowledge bar (Clause 8.3).** This would bar any claim for matters the Buyer or its advisers knew of, or could have discovered from the data room or public records. The Buyer's knowledge is not a complete answer for the Seller here, since the Buyer has now identified the known issues in these documents. However, the clause would bar claims on exactly the matters the Buyer is most likely to face. Australian law on whether a buyer's knowledge bars a warranty claim is not settled and depends on the wording, so the Buyer should insist on express pro-sandbagging language: the Buyer may claim whether or not it knew of the matter. Known matters should be dealt with through specific indemnities and price adjustments, not warranty claims.

---

## 3. Known matters (the core of the risk)

The quantifiable items below total about **AUD 4.13m** (Riverlark 3.2m + Ironquay 0.18m + bonuses 0.42m + supplier renewals 0.33m). This is close to the Seller's AUD 4.8m cap, so it is not a rounding issue. Bluefen (about AUD 3.6m of revenue) and the privacy incident are not yet quantified.

**Bluefen (Clauses 3, 6.3; DD-002; Disclosure 2).** Bluefen accounts for about 30% of FY26 revenue. Change-control consent has not been obtained, and the Seller has not produced the consent or evidence that the conditions in clause 11.3 are satisfied.
- The Seller's proposal to use "reasonable endeavours" and treat the condition as satisfied on delivery of "the counterparty's written consent" is inadequate. Delivery of a consent is not the same as the consent being valid, unconditional, and covering the sale.
- Push for: consent to be a condition precedent (not a reasonable endeavours obligation); the consent to satisfy all clause 11.3 conditions; and a walk right, plus a price adjustment or specific indemnity, if Bluefen terminates or re-prices within a defined period after signing.

**Riverlark (Clauses 2, 7; DD-003; Disclosure 3).** About AUD 3.2m is outstanding and unpaid, and no discharge of security has been provided. The Seller proposes a release "following Completion."
- This is not acceptable. The price is stated as debt-free and cash-free, so the Riverlark debt should be repaid from the price at Completion, not after it.
- Push for: a payout letter from Riverlark showing the amount; repayment at Completion through the funds flow; and release of all security (including PPSR registrations) at Completion, with discharge documents held in escrow beforehand.
- The deal team should also confirm whether the AUD 24m is an enterprise or equity figure. If it is enterprise value, the Riverlark debt is deducted, and the funds flow needs to show it clearly.

**Ironquay IP (Clause 11.1; DD-004; DD-010; Disclosure 4).** The Seller says the existing indemnity is "adequate" because it covers the SOW3 payment. This is not right:
- Under DD-004 clause 7.3, the SOW3 Project Materials do not transfer until every SOW3 fee is paid. The data room shows AUD 180k open. The Disclosure Letter says this is not bank verification of non-payment.
- There is no receipt, no confirmatory assignment, and no confirmation from Ironquay.
- The indemnity does not address title to the materials, IP ownership, or third-party claims.
- Push for: an uncapped specific indemnity covering IP ownership, title to project materials, and unpaid fees; payment of the AUD 180k from Seller proceeds before Completion (or a retention); a confirmatory assignment from Ironquay as a Completion deliverable.

**Employee bonuses (DD-005; Disclosure 5).** AUD 420k of conditional Completion bonuses is not in the draft funds flow, and the disclosure is silent on payroll tax, superannuation, and on-costs.
- Bonuses triggered by the transaction are typically a Seller cost in a debt-free, cash-free deal. They should be treated as transaction expenses or debt-like items and deducted from the price.
- Payroll tax (NSW) and superannuation are likely to apply to these payments, so the Seller should bear them too. The Buyer should not inherit any unpaid bonus or on-cost exposure, and should not pay these amounts if the continued-employment conditions are later contested.

**Privacy and export incident (DD-006; Clause 4.6 and Schedule 6; Disclosure 6).** The Seller calls this a preliminary operational matter. The record describes roughly 1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles, and activity timestamps, sent to an unintended external address. Whether anyone accessed the file, and whether notification is required, has not been established.
- Under Part IIIC of the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable assessment within 30 days. The Seller should confirm when the assessment began and whether it has been completed, and whether notification obligations have been triggered. The data here is largely business contact information, which may reduce the risk, but the Seller has not shown this.
- Push for: a completed forensic assessment and privacy advice before signing; a specific indemnity for all losses arising from the incident, including notification costs, regulatory investigations, and third-party claims, without the general cap or basket; a privacy warranty; and a retention or escrow until the assessment is complete.
- The Seller calling this "not expected to be material" is not a basis for leaving the risk with the Buyer.

**Supplier renewals (DD-008, DD-011; Disclosure 8).** Three renewals total AUD 330k, each at AUD 110k. The Seller calls them ordinary course, but the disclosure does not say whether they are terminable, what the term is, or whether they were entered into before the disclosure date.
- Read together, three identical AUD 110k renewals could be a split to fall under a threshold. The Buyer should check whether they are related and whether they run past Completion.
- Push for: copies of the contracts and termination rights; an interim covenant requiring Buyer consent for new or renewed contracts above a threshold; and treatment as a Seller cost or debt-like item for any committed amounts that are not ordinary course or cannot be terminated.

**Office lease (DD-007; Disclosure 7).** The lease imposes a notification obligation. The Seller has not confirmed whether landlord consent is needed for the share sale.
- Push for: confirmation from the landlord, or a lease estoppel, as a Completion deliverable, plus a warranty that no consent is required beyond that given.

**Mossvale (DD-009; Disclosure 9).** The assignment restriction is not clearly triggered by a sale of shares. The Seller's letter is silent on whether Mossvale consent is required. Push for a written confirmation from the Seller that no consent is required, backed by a specific warranty. If the Buyer's counsel considers a change of control is caught, make consent a condition precedent.

---

## 4. Title and corporate verification (DD-012; Disclosure 10; "Title" in the summary)

The Seller says title to the 100% shares is evidenced by the share register at DD-012. A register entry is useful evidence but is not verification. The Buyer should:
- run an ASIC company extract and check the register of members;
- obtain original share certificates (or confirmation none were issued) and executed transfer forms;
- run PPSR and other encumbrance searches over the shares and the company's assets;
- obtain board and shareholder approvals for the sale;
- ensure the title warranty is fundamental (see section 1).

---

## 5. Tax and IP (Seller summary)

The Seller considers the tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime." They are not. Tax should be dealt with by a separate pre-Completion tax indemnity, not subject to the general cap, basket, or 18-month period. IP warranties should be fully given (ownership, non-infringement, and the Ironquay materials) and should not be subject to the general cap unless the Buyer agrees otherwise as part of a trade.

---

## Summary of recommendations

**Must-have (non-negotiable):**
1. Reject general disclosure of the data room and public registers. Disclosure must be specific and fair, and the disclosure letter must be brought down to signing and Completion.
2. Reject the "all Claims" time limit and cap structure. Title, capacity, and tax claims must sit outside the general cap and basket and survive longer.
3. Carve out fraud from the exclusive-remedy, limitation, and non-reliance clauses.
4. Reject the Clause 8.3 knowledge bar. Include express pro-sandbagging language.
5. Riverlark: repay at Completion through the funds flow, with discharge of security at Completion.
6. Bluefen: make the consent a condition precedent, with a walk right and a price or indemnity remedy if it is not obtained or is re-priced.
7. Specific, uncapped indemnities for the Ironquay IP, the privacy incident, and any Bluefen loss; Seller to pay the AUD 180k Ironquay amount before Completion or fund a retention.
8. Treat the AUD 420k bonuses, plus payroll tax and super, as a Seller cost, deducted from the price.

**Strong asks:**
9. General cap at a minimum of 100% of the price (or a compromise with a clear trade).
10. Tipping basket, reduced de minimis, and aggregation of related claims.
11. General warranty survival of 36 months; tax to the ATO period plus 60 days; title and capacity for at least six years.
12. Fundamental warranties capped at the full price.
13. Completed privacy assessment before signing.
14. Landlord confirmation or estoppel for the office lease; Mossvale confirmation.
15. Supplier contracts reviewed; interim covenant on new or renewed contracts; Seller cost for non-ordinary-course commitments.

**Verification (before signing):**
16. ASIC, PPSR, and share-register verification of title, plus original share certificates and transfer forms.
17. Full review of DD-002 to DD-012 against the warranties, and an updated data room index at signing.

**Points to confirm with counsel:**
- whether the AUD 24m is an enterprise or equity figure, and how the Riverlark debt is treated;
- the current status of the Privacy Act assessment timetable for DD-006;
- the NSW position on sandbagging and on the drafting needed to exclude fraud, and whether the SPA should be a deed.

The Seller says title to the 100% shares is evidenced by the share register at DD-012. A register entry is useful evidence but is not verification. The Buyer should:
- run an ASIC company extract and check the register of members;
- obtain original share certificates (or confirmation none were issued) and executed transfer forms;
- run PPSR and other encumbrance searches over the shares and the company's assets;
- obtain board and shareholder approvals for the sale;
- ensure the title warranty is fundamental (see section 1).

---

## 5. Tax and IP (Seller summary)

The Seller considers the tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime." They are not. Tax should be dealt with by a separate pre-Completion tax indemnity, not subject to the general cap, basket, or 18-month period. IP warranties should be fully given (ownership, non-infringement, and the Ironquay materials) and should not be subject to the general cap unless the Buyer agrees otherwise as part of a trade.

## Summary of recommendations

**Must-have (non-negotiable):**
1. Reject general disclosure of the data room and public registers. Disclosure must be specific and fair, and the disclosure letter must be brought down to signing and Completion.
2. Reject the "all Claims" time limit and cap structure. Title, capacity, and tax claims must sit outside the general cap and basket and survive longer.
3. Carve out fraud from the exclusive-remedy, limitation, and non-reliance clauses.
4. Reject the Clause 8.3 knowledge bar. Include express pro-sandbagging language.
5. Riverlark: repay at Completion through the funds flow, with discharge of security at Completion.
6. Bluefen: make the consent a condition precedent, with a walk right and a price or indemnity remedy if it is not obtained or is re-priced.
7. Specific, uncapped indemnities for the Ironquay IP, the privacy incident, and any Bluefen loss; Seller to pay the AUD 180k Ironquay amount before Completion or fund a retention.
8. Treat the AUD 420k bonuses, plus payroll tax and super, as a Seller cost, deducted from the price.

**Strong asks:**
9. General cap at a minimum of 100% of the price (or a compromise with a clear trade).
10. Tipping basket, reduced de minimis, and aggregation of related claims.
11. General warranty survival of 36 months; tax to the ATO period plus 60 days; title and capacity for at least six years.
12. Fundamental warranties capped at the full price.
13. Completed privacy assessment before signing.
14. Landlord confirmation or estoppel for the office lease; Mossvale confirmation.
15. Supplier contracts reviewed; interim covenant on new or renewed contracts; Seller cost for non-ordinary-course commitments.

**Verification (before signing):**
16. ASIC, PPSR, and share-register verification of title, plus original share certificates and transfer forms.
17. Full review of DD-002 to DD-012 against the warranties, and an updated data room index at signing.

**Points to confirm with counsel:**
- whether the AUD 24m is an enterprise or equity figure, and how the Riverlark debt is treated;
- the current status of the Privacy Act assessment timetable for DD-006;
- the NSW position on sandbagging and on the drafting needed to exclude fraud, and whether the SPA should be a deed.
